text: Every aggregate function so far has produced exactly one number for the entire table. But a much more common real question is one number PER GROUP — the average price per color, not one single average lumping everything together. That's what GROUP BY is for.

Color, average of list price, as average price, from Production dot Product, group by color. Run this, and instead of one overall average, you get one row per distinct color, each with its own average price.

Here's the mental model, in three steps. Split the table into groups, one group per distinct color. Aggregate separately within each group — average of list price runs once PER group, not once overall. And combine the results into one row per group. Split, aggregate, combine — that's GROUP BY, every time.

And here's the single most important rule, and the source of most beginner errors: every non-aggregated column in your SELECT list has to appear in GROUP BY too. Add Name here, and it fails — because multiple products, with different names, all share the same color group. There's no single, unambiguous name SQL Server could show for that group. Every SELECT column needs to be either wrapped in an aggregate function, or listed in GROUP BY itself.
Split, aggregate, combine — and every non-aggregated column has to be part of the grouping. Next lesson: grouping by more than one column at once. See you there.
